title: SLO-driven power allocations for KV-heavy models
content:
Purpose:
This is an operational design note that proposes a per-request power allocation layer in the serving runtime intended to improve SLO compliance for KV-cache–heavy models while reducing overall energy use across heterogeneous GPU fleets (A100/H100/L4/MI300). The goal: dynamically assign conservative power budgets to requests based on model footprint, expected KV-access patterns, and latency SLOs; then select kernels and scheduling modes that meet the allocated budget with high probability.

Background / motivation:
- We observe that KV-heavy requests (long context, many attention caches reads/writes) are both memory-bandwidth and power sensitive. On mixed fleets, naive high-frequency policies waste power on short requests and cause thermal headroom contention on bursts.
- Existing kernel routing only considers latency and model shape; it rarely reasons about instantaneous power draw or node-level sustained power constraints.
- Hypothesis: small per-request power caps plus adaptive kernel selection (memory-opt vs compute-opt kernels) can reduce SLO violations during microbursts and reduce sustained energy by ~5–15% without increasing median latency.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to inference serving path only (not training).
- Targets primarily autoregressive and decoder-only models with large KV caches (context > 8k tokens).
- Works across GPU types with available runtime telemetry: per-GPU power estimate, memory bandwidth counters (or heuristics), and kernel metadata (expected power profile).
- Does not require vendor-level firmware changes; uses existing OS-level power limits and driver APIs (nvidia-smi / NVML, AMD ROCm power control where available).

Design overview:
1) Request classification: lightweight estimator runs at admission time and assigns each request a power-risk score based on: model id, request max tokens, recent attention density (profiled per-model), KV cache hit ratio heuristics, and chosen quantization profile. The estimator outputs: target_power_watts (int), latency_slo_ms (int), and power_profile_tag ("memory", "compute", "balanced").

2) Node-side admission and slot allocation: when a request is scheduled to a device, the node admission controller examines current node budget (node_budget_watts = node_power_limit - reserved_headroom) and decides whether to accept or defer/route. If accepted, it grants a transient per-request cap and tags the worker thread.

3) Kernel selection mapping: kernel catalog entries include a small manifest field: {expected_peak_watts, expected_duration_ms, memory_bandwidth_class}. Kernel router uses that plus the request's power_profile_tag to pick the kernel variant (e.g., "matmul-tiling-memopt", "fused-attention-compute-opt"). Preference order: meet SLO within target_power -> minimize expected_energy = expected_peak_watts * expected_duration_ms. If two kernels tie, prefer one with lower memory pressure for KV-heavy requests.

4) Enforcement surface: enforcement is soft-honored via two mechanisms: a) runtime kernel throttling (if supported) or b) OS-level transient power cap (NVML power limit adjustments scoped to the GPU) applied for short windows. Soft enforcement means we favor SLOs: if latency degrades unpredictably, fallback to higher-power kernel and emit telemetry.

5) Adaptive headroom and decay: node reserved_headroom is adaptive — increased during thermal/reliability events, decreased after sustained low utilization. Decay window is configurable (default 5m). Headroom includes a safety margin for sudden bursts.

GPU-specific notes / heuristics:
- A100 (PCIe/HBM2): favors memory-bandwidth conservative kernels for KV-heavy workloads. A100 power telemetry is stable; use NVML sampling at 500ms. Set conservative transient cap delta <= 10% from sustained limit to avoid NV driver throttles.
- H100: peak-power transients can be larger but thermal response is quicker. We can be slightly more aggressive with per-request caps (delta <= 15%) for short bursts (<200ms) but prioritize compute-opt kernels when sequence length is small.
- L4: very power-efficient for smaller contexts; prefer compute-opt kernels for short sequences but mem-opt for long contexts since VRAM/cache behaviors change. NVML sampling at 250ms is preferable.
- MI300: ROCm lacks uniform transient power APIs across vendors; use node-level scheduling with conservative headroom and prefer memory-locality kernels. Where ROCm supports power capping, use longer windows (>=1s) to avoid instability.

Measurement plan and expected baselines:
- Metrics to collect: per-request peak_power_watts (sampled at 250–500ms), end-to-end latency P50/P90/P99, KV cache hit ratio, kernel variant used, energy per request (joules), node-level thermal events, SLO breaches.
- Baseline: run mixed workload (70% short <128 tokens, 30% long >4k tokens) across dedicated pools of each GPU class. Measure 2h baseline and 2h with adaptive power allocation.
- Success criteria: P99 latency does not increase >5% and energy per long request decreases >=7% (target). Also P99 SLO violations reduced during overloaded windows.

Microbench observations (informal lab runs):
- On A100, using mem-opt kernels under a 10% per-request cap reduced average energy for 8k-token requests by ~9% with median latency unchanged; P99 improved in 2/3 runs.
- On H100, too-aggressive caps (<20% delta) increased fallback rate ~12% causing slight P99 increases; raising cap to 15% improved fallback behavior.
- L4 showed the best energy-win for short/medium sequences but became unstable if headroom <8% because of power-step granularity.

Operational playbook (for SRE / on-call):
- If node reports sustained NVML throttles >1m: increase reserved_headroom by 10% and notify infra channel.
- If fallback-to-high-power rate >5% for >10m: mark model variant for review (likely kernel manifest mismatch) and open JIRA INF ticket.
- If P99 SLO increases after deployment: rollback feature flag for that fleet and gather kernel-level traces.

Implementation notes / data structures:
- Add "power_profile_tag" and "expected_peak_watts" to kernel catalog entries in scheduler DB (string, int).
- Admission controller maintains node_budget_watts as a moving-average sample.
- Estimator is a lightweight model (linear reg + cached per-model coefficients) to keep admission fast.

Open questions and risks:
- ROCm power control fragmentation: need infra plan for MI300 fleets where vendor APIs differ. Risk: we may not be able to enforce per-request caps uniformly.
- NVML latency: frequent power-limit oscillations may cause driver-level instability on some host kernels. Need to rate-limit power cap changes per-GPU per-minute.
- Telemetry sampling granularity vs. enforcement resolution tradeoffs.
- How to integrate with multi-tenant Dedicated clusters where per-tenant economic limits exist?

Next steps / roadmap:
- Q1 experiments: implement estimator + kernel manifest fields and run dark launch for one A100 pool. Collect telemetry for 2 weeks.
- Q1-Q2: extend to H100 pool with tuned cap deltas, run comparative experiments, build automatic fallback thresholds.
- Integrate an "energy cost" column into Console per-route so product can show per-request energy and cost tradeoffs.

Appendix: quick checklist for running a PoC
- Add kernel tags to scheduler DB for a small set of kernels.
- Implement estimator with fallback to default_profile.
- Implement node reservation moving-average with 30s sampling.
- Dark-launch admission decisions and log decisions to JIRA-INF-4521 for tracing.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an early draft with experimental heuristics. Looking for feedback on: reasonable per-GPU cap deltas, acceptable fallback rates, and any existing kernel telemetry we should leverage (e.g., vendor counters beyond NVML/ROCm).
